file_name: Nystrom DT - 2018 - Methods for Patient Centered Interface Design of Test Result Display in Online Portals.txt

barriers.description: The team used a semi-structured design process without a strict schedule, which sped production but reduced experimental rigor and produced heterogeneous testing stimuli.
barriers.justification: This process-level constraint limited the designers' ability to perform rigorous evaluation and to integrate feedback consistently across iterations, hindering evaluate designs and integrate feedback & iteration workloads.
barriers.reference_excerpt: In the current study, we chose to implement a semi-structured design process that refrained from using a strict schedule to determine when to begin testing and making interface improvements during the design of the interface. This methodology increased the speed at which the interface could be produced at the cost of rigorous experimental design.

barriers.description: The user testing had a low sample size, limiting the statistical and generalizable strength of evaluation findings.
barriers.justification: A small participant pool constrained the designers' ability to evaluate designs comprehensively and to draw reliable conclusions needed for subsequent iteration and specification of requirements.
barriers.reference_excerpt: Aside from a low sample size, the main limitation of the user testing portion of our evaluation is the lack of a homologous "stimuli" to test with participants.

barriers.description: Participant sample was unrepresentative: 71% had prior health-care work experience and all reported some familiarity with the tests shown.
barriers.justification: This interactional bias limited designers' ability to manage authentic user understanding and to facilitate involvement of typical (naïve) patients, reducing the validity of insights used to specify user requirements and evaluate designs.
barriers.reference_excerpt: An additional limitation that may affect the generalizability of the results of this study is the large percentage (71 percent) of patients who had history of working in health care prior to participating in this study. ... All participants indicated they had some familiarity with the tests presented in the test result interface.

barriers.description: Each participant was allowed to use only one version of the interface and could not participate in later sessions.
barriers.justification: This recruitment/design choice prevented designers from tracking how individual users responded across iterations, making it harder to integrate feedback longitudinally and to evaluate the effects of changes across versions.
barriers.reference_excerpt: To avoid skewing the perceptions and results of the later versions of the test result interface, participants were only invited to use one version of the interface and were not allowed to participate again after their initial testing session.

barriers.description: Design changes produced non-linear visual scales, but the team did not assess the impact of these non-linear scales on patient perceptions.
barriers.justification: Failing to evaluate this design consequence limited the designers' ability to understand contextual effects and holistic experience, constraining the evaluate designs and integrate feedback & iteration workloads.
barriers.reference_excerpt: An unanticipated consequence of this design adjustment was the creation of non-linear scales, where the visual space for each biomarker are radically different than the other. We did not make any attempt to assess the impact of these non-linear scales on patient perceptions.

barriers.description: The interface used a red/green color scheme but the study did not include confirmed colorblind participants to evaluate accessibility.
barriers.justification: This oversight limited designers' ability to evaluate and address accessibility in the real context of use, hindering the evaluate designs and address holistic experience workloads.
barriers.reference_excerpt: An additional limitation ... the use of red/green color schemes for the design of our interface could potentially limit the ease of using this interface for colorblind patients. While to our knowledge none of the test subjects were red/green color blind, we should note that "color" was not the only indicator that subjects had available to help them understand the meaning of the graphs or displays.
